criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household/population drinking water service access, intermittent supply, and city-wide supply-demand deficits across four Ethiopian cities (Addis Ababa, Adama, Mekelle, and Dire Dawa).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper briefly discusses institutional and governance challenges in Sections 4.1.8 and 4.2.5 (weak monitoring and O&M capacity, regional water bureau control over project financing/structure versus decentralized municipal enterprises in Adama, weak institutional coordination, inadequate customer service, and inconvenient office bill settlement). However, under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is not met (no): the study's empirical analysis models hydraulic, technical, and water-resource factors (population growth, NRW, nodal pressures, PRVs, demand-saving fixtures, and rainwater harvesting), while the brief governance subsection presents generic utility operational/project-delivery capacity issues and unanalysed macro-governance decentralization background rather than examining a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, administrative burden, discretion, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership rules governing access).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains quantitative empirical and engineering simulation evidence using utility production/consumption records, WHO/JMP statistics, field-measured nodal pressures and chlorine residuals for model calibration, and WaterGEMS hydraulic/water-quality modeling across four cities (though the brief institutional/governance observations lack any documented qualitative sample or analytic method).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports city-level percentage of population with access to drinking water from the urban water supply system (Table 2: 66.11% in Addis Ababa, 78.94% in Adama, 51.58% in Mekelle, 94.43% in Dire Dawa), water supply deficits (MLD), intermittent supply, and node-level pressure-dependent water shortages.
criterion_notes.c5: While city/network units of analysis and technical engineering exposures/outcomes (nodal pressure, PRVs, RWH, demand-side conservation, supply-demand gap) are identifiable, no rule-type legal, administrative, or governance exposure is operationalized or linked to an access outcome, and the key informant interviews mentioned for institutional issues have no reported sample size, respondent roles, or analytic design.

evidence_quotes.quote: Further, the case study noticed that in Addis Ababa alone, potable water is only accessible to 66% of the city population. A significant water supply deficit was observed in Mekelle city, where only half of the city population has access to potable water from the system.

Specifically, it focuses (1) on assessing the water supply and demand gaps, (2) on determining the water loss/unaccountable water, (3) on identifying the low and high pressure as well as water deficit nodes in the WDN, (3) to investigate the water quality problem in WDN, (4) to study the environmental, institutional and governance problem in Ethiopia and (5) proposes sustainable interventions to improve the same through the case studies of four major cities such as Addis Ababa, Adama, Mekelle, and Dire Dawa.

The other primary data has been collected for this study, including measured field data (i.e., mainly nodal pressure and residual chlorine concentration for a selected junction in the AA and DD network).
The current water supply is too low to meet the demand, and the coverage is low (i.e., it does not sufficiently supply some parts of the cities).
The absence of proper monitoring systems coupled with low operation and maintenance capacity is among the main institutional problems in Ethiopia’s UDWS.

Generally, the results obtained from field visits and key informative interviews revealed that the cities in the case studies lacked citizen participation, weak institutional coordination, and lack of awareness.

raw_response.exposure: Technical, hydroclimatic, and water-management factors (population/urbanization demand growth, nodal hydraulic pressures and pipe velocities, non-revenue water/leakage, pressure-reducing valves, demand-side fixture efficiency, rainwater harvesting, source pollution), alongside unanalysed macro-governance decentralization and generic utility operational capacity background
raw_response.outcome: City-level drinking water supply coverage (% of population with access to water supply), daily water supply-demand deficit (MLD), non-revenue water (%), and node-level pressure-dependent water shortage and residual chlorine concentration
raw_response.population_and_sample: Four Ethiopian cities and their urban drinking water systems: Addis Ababa (2021 population 5,060,000; 123 modeled WDN junctions in Yeka and Bole sub-cities), Adama (population 394,000), Mekelle (population 544,000), and Dire Dawa (population 426,000; 168 modeled WDN junctions in Sabian/Zone 2); sample size and characteristics of key informants not reported
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper reports city-level drinking water supply coverage and deficits across four Ethiopian cities (c1=yes, c4=yes) using utility records, field hydraulic/chlorine measurements, and WaterGEMS network simulations (c3=yes), its empirical analysis examines technical engineering and water-resource management interventions (pressure-reducing valves, pipe velocities, booster chlorination, non-revenue water, fixture efficiency, and rainwater harvesting). Its brief discussion of institutional and governance issues (Sections 4.1.8 and 4.2.5) consists of generic operational/project-delivery capacity issues and unanalysed macro-governance decentralization background (with no documented qualitative interview sample or methods linking any governance factor to service access), rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification.
raw_response.study_design: Multi-city technical and descriptive case study combining secondary utility/WHO data, geometric demand projection, WaterGEMS hydraulic and water-quality network simulation, rainwater-harvesting estimation, field observations, and unspecified key informant interviews
